en: To have all Paris's throats cut
Long live the sound, long live the sound
Long live the sound of the cannon!
To be faithful to his country;
Let us give no more quarter.
To make us fall on our arse;
Her husband, believing himself the victor,
To the Temple, into the tower.
That they would fire on our friends;
But how they were blown up,
He said that it would take little
For him to be in that place.
All the good people of the country;
But they will hold each other up
All at the sound of the cannon.
They will stand by them for you
That it would support the country
At the sound of the cannoneer.
Friends, let us always stay united
Let us not fear our enemies
If they come to attack us,
Yes, I am a sans-culotte, I am
In spite of the king's friends
Let us drink to their health;
notes: line 1.1, 3.1: 'Madame Véto' and 'Monsieur Véto' are Marie Antoinette and Louis XVI, named for the king's veto.
line 2.2: 'le son' is the sound (of the cannon, as line 2.4 says).
line 5.3: 'paour' is old popular French for a lout or peasant; the sense is not certain.
line 5.4: the Temple, the fortress in Paris where the royal family was imprisoned in August 1792.
line 6.3-6.4: 'sauter' and 'danser' are slang for being blown up or killed: the Swiss Guards killed at the Tuileries, 10 August 1792.
line 9.3: 'se soutiendront' can also mean 'will stand firm'.
line 10.3: 'vous les soutiendront' is ironic: 'they'll back them up for you'.
line 11.3-11.4: the sense is unclear; perhaps the gendarmes did not fail to turn up when the cannon sounded.
line 14.2: the faubourgs, the working districts on the edge of Paris (Saint-Antoine, Saint-Marcel).
line 8.4: 'pour peu' here: it would take little (for him to lie in the pit being dug).
